variants.title: Convert traffic to capacity units
variants.context: One write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB. A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB costs one read capacity unit; an eventually consistent read of the same size costs half.
variants.prompt: Items are 3.5 KB. The application writes 200 items per second. How many write capacity units does that need?
variants.hint: Round the item size up to whole kilobytes first.
variants.explanation: 3.5 KB rounds up to 4 WCU per write. 4 × 200 = 800 WCU.

mistakes.feedback: Write units round item size up: 3.5 KB costs 4 units, not 3.5.
Each write of a 3.5 KB item costs more than one unit.

variants.title: Convert traffic to capacity units
variants.context: One write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB. A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB costs one read capacity unit; an eventually consistent read of the same size costs half.
variants.prompt: Items are 6 KB. The application performs 100 strongly consistent reads per second. How many read capacity units does that need?
variants.hint: A strongly consistent read covers 4 KB per unit; round up.
variants.explanation: 6 KB needs 2 units per strongly consistent read. 2 × 100 = 200 RCU.

mistakes.feedback: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 rounds up to 2 units per read.
A 6 KB item exceeds the 4 KB covered by one unit.
Read units are per 4 KB, not per kilobyte.

variants.title: Convert traffic to capacity units
variants.context: One write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB. A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB costs one read capacity unit; an eventually consistent read of the same size costs half.
variants.prompt: Items are 4 KB. The application performs 300 eventually consistent reads per second. How many read capacity units does that need?
variants.hint: An eventually consistent read costs half of a strongly consistent one.
variants.explanation: A 4 KB strongly consistent read is 1 RCU, so eventually consistent is 0.5. 0.5 × 300 = 150 RCU.

mistakes.feedback: That is the strongly consistent cost; eventual consistency halves it.
Read units cover 4 KB each, and eventual reads cost half.

variants.title: Explain the throttle
variants.context: A table with ample aggregate capacity still throttles when one partition-key value or GSI key range receives too much work. Each partition is designed for up to 1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU per second.
variants.prompt: A table has 10,000 WCU provisioned and uses only 3,000, yet writes to one customer ID are throttled. Why?
options: The provisioned capacity figure was entered incorrectly.
On-demand mode is required before any burst is allowed.
That partition key exceeds the per-partition write ceiling.
optionFeedback: The table has plenty of unused units; the issue is distribution.
On-demand still has per-partition limits and hot-key pressure.
Each partition is designed for up to 1,000 WCU, whatever the table totals say.
variants.hint: Where does a single key’s traffic land?
variants.explanation: Aggregate capacity and hot-key pressure are separate. Adaptive capacity helps, but a single key cannot exceed its partition’s ceiling.

variants.title: Explain the throttle
variants.context: A table with ample aggregate capacity still throttles when one partition-key value or GSI key range receives too much work. Each partition is designed for up to 1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU per second.
variants.prompt: Customer IDs distribute perfectly, but a GSI keyed on status = OPEN throttles, and now base-table writes are throttled too. Why?
options: A GSI draws on table capacity and has no ceiling of its own.
The base table has run out of storage on that partition.
The low-cardinality GSI key is hot and back-pressures the table.
optionFeedback: A GSI has its own partitions and its own capacity ceilings.
Storage is not the signal here; write distribution on the index is.
Every index is its own distribution surface, and a hot index partition throttles the base write.
variants.hint: The base table and each index distribute independently.
variants.explanation: A GSI with a few key values concentrates its writes. If the index cannot keep up, DynamoDB throttles the base-table write to protect index consistency.

variants.title: Explain the throttle
variants.context: A table with ample aggregate capacity still throttles when one partition-key value or GSI key range receives too much work. Each partition is designed for up to 1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU per second.
variants.prompt: A team switches to on-demand mode to fix hot-key throttling. What should they expect?
options: Hot key ranges can still throttle under on-demand.
All throttling disappears as soon as the mode changes.
Reads also become strongly consistent by default.
optionFeedback: On-demand removes the table-level target but keeps per-partition limits and quotas.
Capacity mode does not change how a single key is placed.
Consistency is chosen per read, not by capacity mode.
variants.hint: Which limit does the capacity mode actually change?
variants.explanation: On-demand is a strong default for spiky traffic, but a partition-key value that concentrates work still hits its partition’s ceiling.

variants.title: Pick the operation
variants.context: Prefer GetItem when the full primary key is known, Query when a partition key and optional sort-key condition bound the result, and treat Scan as deliberate table-wide work. A FilterExpression runs after items are read.
variants.prompt: You know a customer ID and need their twenty newest orders. The table uses PK = CUSTOMER#id and SK = ORDER#timestamp#id. Which call?
options: Query on the partition key, reading in reverse sort order.
A Scan with a FilterExpression on the customer ID.
One GetItem call for each of the twenty orders.
optionFeedback: A Query bounds the result to one item collection and sorts by the sort key.
A Scan reads the whole table and filters afterwards.
GetItem needs each full key, and you do not know the order IDs yet.
variants.hint: Which call names one partition and a bounded range?
variants.explanation: Query is the tool for “one partition key plus a sort-key condition”. It returns only the matching item collection.

variants.title: Pick the operation
variants.context: Prefer GetItem when the full primary key is known, Query when a partition key and optional sort-key condition bound the result, and treat Scan as deliberate table-wide work. A FilterExpression runs after items are read.
variants.prompt: A report needs every order over $500 across all customers. The table has no index on amount. What is true of a Scan with FilterExpression amount > 500?
options: It reads only the items where the amount exceeds 500.
It reads every item and filters afterwards, paying for all reads.
It costs about as much as a key lookup, since filtering is server-side.
optionFeedback: DynamoDB cannot know which items match without reading them.
Filters run after candidate items are read, so the cost is the full read.
Server-side filtering does not turn a broad read into a key lookup.
variants.hint: When does the filter run relative to the read?
variants.explanation: A FilterExpression narrows the response, not the work. Model the query with a key or index if it is a real access pattern.

variants.title: Pick the operation
variants.context: Prefer GetItem when the full primary key is known, Query when a partition key and optional sort-key condition bound the result, and treat Scan as deliberate table-wide work. A FilterExpression runs after items are read.
variants.prompt: You have the complete primary key of one order and need the whole item. Which call?
options: Scan with a limit of one item.
GetItem with that key.
Query with a filter on order ID.
optionFeedback: Scan is table-wide work; a limit of one does not make it a lookup.
A known full key is exactly what GetItem is for.
Query works but is indirect; GetItem is the direct contract for a full key.
variants.hint: Is the full primary key known?
variants.explanation: Prefer GetItem when the complete primary key is known. It is the cheapest and most direct access path.

variants.title: Model from the access pattern
variants.context: DynamoDB modeling starts from access patterns: name each operation, define its bounds, assign keys and indexes, then test skew and failure with realistic data.
variants.prompt: A new commerce table is being designed. Put the modeling steps in order.

items.text: Load-test realistic key distributions, retries, GSI pressure, and restores.
Define result count, item size, freshness, atomicity, peak rate, and retention for each.
Assign base keys, sort-key ranges, and secondary indexes to each operation.
Name each concrete operation, such as “get order by ID”.

variants.hint: DynamoDB reverses relational habits: operations first, tables later.
variants.explanation: Operations → bounds → keys and indexes → proof under skew and failure. Normalizing entities first leads to queries the keys cannot serve.

variants.title: Model from the access pattern
variants.context: DynamoDB modeling starts from access patterns: name each operation, define its bounds, assign keys and indexes, then test skew and failure with realistic data.
variants.prompt: A team is migrating a relational schema to DynamoDB. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Test skew, concurrency races, and restore procedures with production-shaped data.
Record the bounds of each request: size, freshness, rate, and isolation.
Map identity to base keys, relationships to sort keys, and alternate lookups to indexes.
List the application’s reads and writes as concrete requests.

variants.hint: You cannot pick keys before you know what they must answer.
variants.explanation: Start from the access patterns, bound them, then choose keys and prove them. Single-table design is a technique, not the goal.

variants.title: Model from the access pattern
variants.context: DynamoDB modeling starts from access patterns: name each operation, define its bounds, assign keys and indexes, then test skew and failure with realistic data.
variants.prompt: An existing table throttles under a new feature. Put the redesign steps in order.

items.text: Load-test the new keys against realistic skew before shipping.
Define their peak rate, result shape, and consistency needs.
Choose the key or GSI that serves each with well-distributed partition values.
Write down the new operations the feature actually issues.

variants.hint: Even a redesign starts with naming the operations.
variants.explanation: The same loop applies to changes: name, bound, model, prove. Skipping the last step is how hot keys reach production.

variants.title: Protect the invariant
variants.context: A strongly consistent pre-read does not lock an item. Conditional writes reject a mutation when the current item no longer satisfies a version, existence, state, or numeric invariant; transactions group items into one all-or-nothing operation.
variants.prompt: Two workers read an order in state pending, then both try to mark it paid. How do you prevent a double transition?
options: Retry the update in a loop until it succeeds.
Use a condition expression requiring status pending.
Do a strongly consistent read first, then update.
optionFeedback: Retrying a blind update just repeats the same unconditional write.
The condition is checked atomically at mutation time, so the second update is rejected.
A pre-read does not lock; both workers can read pending and both can write.
variants.hint: Which check happens at the same instant as the write?
variants.explanation: Enforce the invariant in the write itself. A condition expression or transaction rejects the stale transition; a pre-read cannot.

variants.title: Protect the invariant
variants.context: A single PutItem, UpdateItem, or DeleteItem is atomic for its item. TransactWriteItems groups multiple item actions into one ACID operation that commits or cancels as a unit.
variants.prompt: Placing an order must debit inventory and create the order item together, or not at all. Which mechanism?
options: TransactWriteItems across both items.
Two separate UpdateItem calls with retries.
A single UpdateItem on the order with a condition on inventory.
optionFeedback: A transaction commits or cancels both actions together.
Two calls can leave one applied and the other failed.
A condition on one item cannot read or change a different item atomically.
variants.hint: How many items must change together?
variants.explanation: Cross-item atomicity needs a transaction. Single-item calls are atomic only for their own item.

variants.title: Protect the invariant
variants.context: Transient throttling is part of the API contract. A reliable client backs off, retries only safe work, and keeps a stable identifier so a retry refers to the same business operation.
variants.prompt: A Lambda consumer of a DynamoDB stream charges a card per change record. A batch fails halfway and is retried. What prevents double charges?
options: Reading the stream records with strong consistency.
An idempotency boundary keyed by a stable operation ID.
A larger batch size so that fewer batches fail.
optionFeedback: Streams are delivered at least once, and read consistency does not deduplicate.
Retried batches redeliver records, so the destination must recognize work it already did.
Batch size changes throughput, not duplicate delivery.
variants.hint: What happens to the records in a retried batch?
variants.explanation: Stream consumers still need destination-side idempotency, because failed batches are retried and records arrive again.
